criterion_scores.reasoning: The main control flow is sound: session gating, transcript-derived counts, record construction, and optional projection all line up with the in-file contract. I checked the write path, and the only substantive issue is that the append result is not verified, so an I/O failure can lose the authoritative record silently.

I checked the full expected pipeline stages and found no missing sections, TODO stubs, or omitted load-bearing behavior. The artifact includes gating, metadata extraction, record emission, and the optional adapter path.
I checked placement/name conventions for a `.claude/hooks/` shell hook, the shebang, and the absence of forbidden naming patterns. Nothing stood out as a house-convention violation.

I checked for ceremony, duplicated state, hardcoded secrets, and tombstoned platform choices. The implementation stays lean and uses the sanctioned authoritative JSONL plus derived projection pattern.

The script is readable, but failure reporting is weak: the PostHog call is silenced completely, and the authoritative write path has no success check. That makes operational failures hard to diagnose even though the control flow is otherwise clear.

defects.description: The authoritative append is not checked. Because the script does not use `set -e` and does not test the write result, a permission/full-disk/filesystem error can drop the build-session record silently, contradicting the 'ALWAYS append' contract in the header comment.

All projection failures are fully suppressed, so network/auth/5xx problems disappear without any signal. That makes missing telemetry hard to explain or triage even though the hook is otherwise acting as a telemetry emitter.

Compared the script against the contract comments in the file (always append authoritative record; PostHog only when key is set; content-gated counts only).
Reviewed the jq parsing/defensive-default branches for malformed or missing transcript data.
Checked hook placement/naming and shell header conventions for obvious convention issues.
